paragraphs: President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is looking into Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's affair with a woman US intelligence officials reportedly believe was a Chinese spy. Trump said he phoned Huang that day and asked whether he knew. "He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. He did not elaborate on the probe or say when it began, and the FBI declined to comment to the BBC.

According to a New York Times report cited by the BBC, US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, worked for Beijing. She was managing director of the Singapore company Megaspeed, which has dealt with Nvidia, and is not related to Jensen Huang. The Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials last spring warning of the relationship. Asked when he learned of it, Trump said he was informed "over a period of time" but gave no specifics.

China's foreign ministry rejected the claims as "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife and apologized. He said he would cooperate with an independent investigation commissioned by Nvidia's board, which said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. Alice Huang has not publicly commented, according to Al Jazeera.

Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, wiping about $250 billion off its value, according to the BBC. Huang and Nvidia were also sued in a proposed class action in California alleging they concealed his ties to a suspected Chinese spy. The BBC said it had contacted Nvidia about the suit.

Congressional committee chairmen have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia's security protocols. It is unclear whether he will appear. Trump said he was sure Chinese leader Xi Jinping would ask him about the matter when they next meet.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, has come under international scrutiny after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted being unfaithful to his wife, following reports linking him to Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. According to The New York Times, US intelligence officials believe she is a Chinese intelligence asset. Huang's statement did not name her or the company.

CNBC describes Megaspeed as a firm that sells Asia Pacific companies access to computing power hosted in Southeast Asian data centers, and says it advertises itself as a core business partner of Nvidia's cloud computing business in the region. It has offices in Singapore and Indonesia. CNBC noted that US export controls restrict some advanced chip sales to China, but remote access to chips located elsewhere is a separate question.

Megaspeed has faced earlier scrutiny. Bloomberg reported in December 2025 that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether it smuggled Nvidia chips to China. Megaspeed responded on its website that the article contained misleading information and said inspections by the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, Malaysian authorities and Nvidia found no evidence of violations.

A House Select Committee on China statement on Nov. 5 called Alice Huang a publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset. Bloomberg reports she also goes by Huang Le and helped set up Megaspeed in 2023. Singapore's government has said it had not investigated her alleged intelligence ties or her relationship with Jensen Huang.

Committee leaders have asked Huang to attend a Nov. 18 briefing on the extent to which US national security may have been put at risk. Nvidia said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and its board's inquiry will examine all available information. CNBC said it had contacted Megaspeed for comment.

The Senate voted 73 to 25 on Monday to invoke cloture on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a bill of roughly 417 pages meant to make it easier to build big infrastructure projects. The vote limits debate and moves the bill toward a final vote, but does not pass it. President Trump urged all senators to back it. It is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats.

According to The Guardian, the bill would simplify federal rules for interstate transmission lines, shorten Endangered Species Act timelines, limit use of the Clean Water Act, narrow reviews under the National Historic Preservation Act and change the National Environmental Policy Act, including what requires review and who can sue. Supporters say projects take too long to build. The Guardian reported that 2,060 GW of generation and storage capacity was waiting to connect to the grid at the end of 2025.

Opposition has come from Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and the ACLU, which say the bill weakens environmental laws and would speed gas pipelines and ICE detention centers. Indigenous groups say it weakens the duty to consult tribes. The National Congress of American Indians' president, Mark Macarro, called it an "existential threat to Indian country." The American Petroleum Institute called it "a historic opportunity."

Democratic sponsors Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse said they had the votes and had made last-minute changes to ensure tribal consultation. Heinrich argued that a level playing field favors clean energy. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the bill "falls short in several areas" and that he would not "rubber-stamp legislation."
The Guardian noted that Democrats elected last week do not take their seats until January, leaving time for the current Congress to act. What the House does remains to be seen.

President Trump said Monday he will "stand by" Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whom the Washington Examiner calls War Secretary, as Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, moved to impeach him. Trump called Massie a "loser." Massie formally introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor Monday, which starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to act. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution, refer it to committee or set it aside.

Massie alleges Hegseth broke the law by engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization. Hegseth has called the effort a "sham," called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman," and said he is not worried. He plans a news conference Tuesday. Trump praised Hegseth's role in the capture of Venezuela's president and said soldiers "love Pete Hegseth."

Massie lost re-election earlier this year and has criticized Trump and the Iran war. The BBC reports he says his aim is to push Trump to replace Hegseth, and a successor could be confirmed while Republicans still control Congress, before Democrats could start their own process in January. Democratic leaders have signaled openness to such an effort.

The BBC said the measure will likely fail. Massie said he was unsure it had enough support. The House has 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats, so it would probably need some Republican votes. Peter Loge, a George Washington University professor, told the BBC he thought it was likely to pass because many Republicans might not show up to vote.

If the House impeached Hegseth, the Senate would hold a trial, and conviction requires a two-thirds vote. The BBC noted the House has impeached only two cabinet members in US history, and the Senate convicted neither.

President Trump said Monday that Iran is "militarily effectively over," after meeting Qatar's prime minister in Washington. Speaking in a surprise briefing, Trump said the US was keeping the "status quo" at the request of Iran's neighbors, which includes continuing a naval blockade of Iranian ports and a new effort, Task Force Iron Gate, to cut off trade by land and through the Caspian Sea. He said he sees momentum toward an end to the conflict that "is going to be ending fairly soon," while the US is "locked and loaded" if needed.

Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, said they discussed ways to progress US-Iran talks. Al Jazeera reported he reportedly presented a two-day proposal from Iran to end the war.

Iranian officials rejected Trump's account. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, wrote on social media that Washington should stop "manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks." President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran is open to more negotiations but "will not surrender to force and bullying," according to Iranian media. He said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had called for an end to a situation he described as "neither war nor peace."

Al Jazeera reports Iranian officials have pushed the US to accept seven conditions to end the war, including lifting sanctions, releasing frozen funds, recognizing a new Hormuz shipping route worked out with Oman, and ending the war on all fronts, including Israel's attacks on Lebanon.

The war began February 28 and has spilled into neighboring countries and disrupted trade. Al Jazeera said US offensive action has become sporadic in recent months, including recent "minor strikes" on Qeshm Island. Trump said a "long-term solution" is needed rather than a short-term one.

Senior officials from Russia, Ukraine and the United States are meeting in Abu Dhabi for the first trilateral talks on ending the war since February. On the eve of the talks, a US official told reporters that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on who would control Ukraine's eastern regions after the war, the BBC reported.

Publicly, the sides remain far apart. Moscow demands that Ukraine give up the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the current line to keep them, saying they are crucial to its security. The US official said the territorial question cannot be solved until the sides know the postwar "security architecture," and that the two issues must be finalized together.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations, crisis communication hotlines and "reciprocal de-escalation measures," and officials floated reactivating the Nato-Russia Council. Jared Kushner, part of the US delegation with envoy Steve Witkoff, said the talks would address both countries' postwar security concerns. He cautioned they could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations."

The last trilateral round, in Geneva in February, produced no breakthrough, and US attention then shifted to the war on Iran. European leaders, largely excluded, want a seat. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged including Nato and EU members in discussions on Europe's security. The US official said Washington would propose a multilateral format, though he acknowledged Russia's distrust of the Europeans.

Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine," which Kyiv would reject. Russia continues to strike Ukraine, including its energy infrastructure.

Anthropic is moving ahead with its planned initial public offering despite a recent tech sell-off, according to The Wall Street Journal as relayed by TechCrunch and CNBC. The Journal reported the company plans to set a valuation range this week and begin trading on Thursday or Friday of next week. CNBC said it is expected to meet with major investors this week.

Valuation is the key question. The Journal reported that some institutional investors are pushing for a valuation below the $1.5 trillion target discussed as recently as last week, which was itself well below the $2 trillion floated a few months ago. CNBC said the potential valuation has reportedly fallen as low as $1 trillion after last week's technology sell-off, amid concerns that the Democratic midterm wave will slow data center construction. By comparison, OpenAI was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after raising $11 billion, short of the $20 billion it sought.

CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday that the offering could be a crucial test of investor confidence in AI. "Without it, I don't see how the AI-related stocks can make a real recovery," he said, calling it possibly "one of the most consequential IPOs in history." Anthropic filed its S-1 paperwork two weeks ago.

Cramer argued that heavy spending on AI chips and data centers depends on a few AI developers earning enough revenue. He pointed to SpaceX, which rents computing capacity to Google and Anthropic. According to Anthropic's prospectus, its monthly commitment has grown from an initial $1.25 billion to more than $3 billion. Cramer said a failed deal could force lower estimates for SpaceX, Nvidia and other suppliers.
The next signals to watch are the valuation range and the debut date.

Qantas said Tuesday it will cut 850 local corporate jobs by outsourcing work to the professional services firm Accenture, with most roles moving to India. The airline said it had signed a multi-year agreement to modernize its back-end systems, processes and data while increasing investment in technology and AI.

In an internal email, CEO Vanessa Hudson said she was sorry for the uncertainty, according to the BBC. She said changes would start in mid-2027 with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles moving mostly to teams in India and some in Australia. Hudson said the airline would consult staff and unions before final decisions. She described the pace of technological change as "unprecedented" and said the decision was "not a reflection of their contribution or commitment."

Hudson said Qantas spends more than AU$1 billion a year on technology and runs on more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together. The company said that in time the work Accenture takes over will be transformed further with automation and AI. Qantas employs about 28,000 people in Australia and 4,000 elsewhere. The BBC said it had contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

The Guardian called it the third major corporate layoff plan in Australia in three weeks, after National Australia Bank, with 2,500 roles, and Canva, with 1,200. It said the changes are expected to draw a strong response from unions that have previously fought Qantas over outsourcing.

The Guardian also noted unemployment is at its highest in nearly five years and that Qantas has been dealing with rising jet fuel prices tied to the Iran conflict, partly offset by new customers. The airline said last week that demand was resilient but it would adjust fares and capacity.

Global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to fall in 2026 for the first time in five years, according to the latest Global Carbon Budget, compiled by more than 140 researchers and reported by New Scientist. About 38.2 gigatonnes are projected, a 0.4 percent decrease from the previous year.

The drop is largely due to a projected 1.9 percent fall in emissions from oil, partly offset by a 0.6 percent rise in emissions from coal. New Scientist attributes the slowdown partly to the energy shock from the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February. Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about 20 percent of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas, pushing up oil prices. That is still affecting petrol prices and household gas bills and has led countries to turn to alternative fuels for energy security.

Robbie Andrew of the CICERO climate research group, a report author, said financial pressure from the shock likely caused the drop, which may prove a "blip." He said that, assuming no further crises, emissions would be expected to bounce back. The outlook depends on how long the shock lasts and on governments weighing the economic case for fossil fuel subsidies.

Renewables also played a part. Electric vehicles, solar and wind are predicted to offset 64 to 79 percent of emissions growth from rising demand through 2028. In China, the largest emitter, emissions are projected to fall 0.9 percent in 2026. Corinne Le Quéré of the University of East Anglia said that if oil prices return to pre-conflict levels, emissions will most likely rebound until renewables accelerate further.
For comparison, the article says emissions fell about 6 percent in 2020 during the pandemic and about 2 percent in 2009 during the financial crisis.

A 16-year-old identified in court only as RK, because of his age, has told the New South Wales Supreme Court that he was radicalised online and used ChatGPT while forming plans for a terrorist attack in Sydney in 2024. He pleaded guilty to acts in preparation for, or planning, a terrorist act. On Monday, Justice Stephen Campbell ordered a three-year community corrections order, so he avoided jail.

RK was just 14 when the offending occurred. He told the court he first saw extremist material on TikTok, starting with historical videos about the crusades, then September 11 and the war on terror, then religious content that led to more violent material. He said he was trying to impress people he spoke with online and became focused on the Sydney Opera House.

According to the Guardian, he sought instructions on making a pressure cooker bomb on Telegram and watched bomb-making videos on YouTube. He used ChatGPT to ask about the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, security arrangements at the Opera House, and where terrorists were imprisoned in New South Wales. He emailed a prison asking whether he could email Tsarnaev but never made contact. Campbell said RK had no concrete plans and had not obtained any bomb-making material.

Campbell said he was satisfied RK had genuinely renounced violent extremism and that deradicalisation was well advanced. RK had completed six sessions of religious and ethical training with a Muslim cleric. OpenAI, Telegram and YouTube were approached for comment, and TikTok declined.

Separately, Claire McGuinness of the intelligence agency Asio told a parliamentary inquiry last month that detecting and disrupting online youth radicalisation had become very challenging. She described young people moving from mainstream platforms to services such as Discord or Telegram.

Wyndham has acknowledged a cybersecurity incident after a security researcher found a password inside the source code of its Android app that gave access to an internal company database hosted by Salesforce, TechCrunch reports.

Researcher Robert Wiggins of What Security said the credential exposed customer names, email addresses and Wyndham member numbers, along with login tokens known as JWTs and company files. He said the database held millions of entries but he could not determine an accurate number of exposed customer records. Wyndham touts some 129 million enrolled rewards members.

Wiggins said Wyndham has no way to report security flaws, so he asked TechCrunch to help alert the company. Soon after TechCrunch contacted Wyndham's cybersecurity staff, the credential was revoked. A spokesperson said, "Our team has taken steps to address the issue," and that security teams "have no evidence of any unauthorized access," without giving details.

The spokesperson would not say whether the company can tell, for example through server logs, if anyone accessed the database before the discovery. The company also would not say whether it will notify customers or disclose the incident to regulators such as the SEC, how long the password was in the app, or whether it will create a vulnerability disclosure program.

Developers generally avoid hardcoding credentials because anyone with a copy of an app can extract them. Wiggins said this was his second such discovery in two weeks, after a similar flaw in Applebee's app, and that he used AI tools to find both. He noted that without visibility into past activity, someone with malicious intent could have leaked large amounts of customer data.

Scott Bright of Bellevue, Washington, lost more than $308,000 on sports wagers on Kalshi and is suing the prediction market for over $580,000, Ars Technica reports. His suit, filed September 24 in King County Superior Court, says Washington has banned online gambling since 2006 and lets people who lose money at illegal gambling recover it from the proprietor.

Bright says he transferred $315,353.94 to Kalshi between June 17 and August 14, 2026, betting on events such as baseball games and tennis matches. He alleges his deposits were cycled through more than $14.4 million in transactions and that Kalshi kept $84,062.71 in trading fees. His net loss was $308,781.62.

Kalshi filed a motion to dismiss on October 30 and wants the case moved to federal court. It argues Bright traded "event contracts" governed by the Commodity Exchange Act and overseen by the CFTC, not gambling. Kalshi also says his losses went to counterparties rather than to Kalshi, and notes he does not allege anyone misled him.

Bright alleges Kalshi's trading affiliate took the opposite side of many of his positions, though he says he does not know for certain because that information is in Kalshi's possession. Kalshi says the affiliate provides liquidity and has access only to the same public information as other traders.

The Ninth Circuit ruled in August that Nevada can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws, and Bright's suit quotes that ruling. Washington's attorney general has a separate suit and won an order restricting certain wagers, effective after Bright's losses. Bright's attorney had not responded to Ars Technica at publication.

On Paramount Skydance's latest earnings call, CEO David Ellison said AI has the potential to be "the biggest creative unlock in modern history," The Verge reports. Asked about the company's outlook for AI, he said it is hard to imagine AI won't have a more significant impact on the film industry than CGI.

Ellison compared the moment to the advent of CGI and digital composites in the early 1990s, which he said gave rise to films such as Jurassic Park and Terminator 2. He said Terminator cost $4 million to make, but that shot for shot today it would cost $60 to 70 million. He suggested AI tools could make budgets "more digestible" so studios can take more risks on original storytelling.

He said AI will "significantly" reshape the company's business and that Paramount Skydance has been developing its own tools. Ellison claimed that as a result, content will be easier to produce, projects across the organization will speed up, and how people work will transform. He added that this makes premium intellectual property and live events more valuable, not less.

Ellison also said that "in a world of AI slop," there will always be a premium for hand-crafted storytelling. He described artificial intelligence as "a tool for artists" that "will never be a replacement for them." The Verge's account rests on his statements during the call; responses from artists or unions were not included in the page text.

Pope Leo XIV met privately with five survivors of clerical sexual abuse in Buenos Aires on Monday, the second day of his visit to Argentina, according to Al Jazeera. The Vatican said the pope spoke individually with each survivor, listened to their painful stories and heard their proposals for strengthening paths toward healing within the Church.

The meeting lasted more than an hour. Leo, 71, reiterated his pledge to strengthen safeguarding in the Catholic Church. The Vatican said these were the first of several talks with survivors planned during his 12-day Latin America tour, which began in Uruguay, continues in Argentina and ends in Peru.

The closed-door meetings followed an open-air mass on Avenida del Libertador that drew an estimated 2.5 million people. Al Jazeera described it as the country's first papal liturgy in nearly 40 years. The visit is the first by a pontiff since Pope John Paul II's trip in 1987.

The Holy See Press Office said in October that the meetings reflect the pope's desire to express closeness to those who have suffered, build paths to healing and ensure the Church is a safe and spiritually healthy place. Leo, the first pope born in the United States, has consistently met with survivors during foreign visits as part of a wider effort to repair relations and restore the Church's credibility after decades of lawsuits, abuse and cover-ups.

Al Jazeera cited figures illustrating the scale of the problem: a 2021 inquiry estimated 216,000 victims of French Catholic clergy between 1950 and 2020, and earlier research counted more than 10,600 people abused by Catholic priests in the United States between 1950 and 2002.

A woman who says Jeffrey Epstein raped her has told the BBC World Service that the model agency representing her put her in danger by sending her to two photoshoots at his Florida beach house. She is identified as Roza. She was 18 and had arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier when MC2 Model Management's US branch first sent her to Epstein's Palm Beach home in 2009. Epstein was then serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work from his home each day.

Roza says MC2's then US president, Jeff Fuller, knew where she was going. She showed the BBC an expense statement suggesting Fuller booked her flight home after the second shoot. The BBC said Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house and has said he did not know she was being abused. He did not respond to the BBC's latest allegations. Roza says the shoots led to a job as Epstein's assistant, and that he then systematically raped her.

The BBC says documents released by the US Department of Justice show 10 MC2 models met or communicated with Epstein after his conviction, and that he gave $1 million to MC2 in 2005. Fuller now runs The Source Models, to which 50 MC2 models were transferred; it did not reply to the BBC.

The BBC also reported that former agent Ramsey Elkholy tried to connect 34 women to Epstein. Elkholy told the BBC he rejects any allegation that he knew of or facilitated abuse and said he meant to help models find opportunities.

New York State senator Zellnor Myrie is challenging a Justice Department statement that no evidence warrants investigating uncharged third parties, and has proposed a bill giving police greater power to investigate alleged enablers.

NASA's Perseverance rover has detected a mineral on Mars that is the same material as ruby, though the mission has not found collectable gemstones, according to a blog post by SuperCam principal investigator Roger Wiens dated November 4, 2026.

Wiens wrote that about two years ago the SuperCam team was startled to see strong, narrow luminescence peaks at wavelengths of 692.7 and 694.1 nanometers when its laser hit a light-colored rock. He said this light comes from delayed atomic transitions in chromium atoms within the structure of corundum. SuperCam can time the delay of the resulting photons, which let the team verify the source. The gemstone form of chromium-containing corundum is ruby. A team led by Ann Ollila published the results in Geophysical Research Letters earlier this year.

Wiens said the team had tested the effect before launch by placing a ruby in the laser beam and watching the room pulse bright red. On Mars, he said, the small corundum crystals are helping scientists learn about the planet's past. Corundum is a metamorphic and pegmatitic mineral that would not be expected on a planet without plate tectonics. Large meteor and asteroid impacts, however, can cause local metamorphism through long-term heating.

Because Perseverance is exploring very ancient terrain near the rim of Jezero crater, Wiens wrote, some evidence of localized metamorphism is expected. He said the team tried the technique only rarely earlier in the mission but has lately used time-resolved luminescence observations frequently on light-toned rocks to look for more evidence of impact effects.
